issues.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that compulsorily requires registration cannot itself create the lease it purports to record or be used as evidence of that lease.
material_facts: The parties executed an instrument purporting to grant a lease for five years.
Neither party relied on an exception in the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act.
issues.conclusion: The instrument could not create the purported five-year lease and could not be used as evidence of a lease created by that instrument.
issues.legal_principle: Section 107, first paragraph, of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, 1908, require registration of leases from year to year, for a term exceeding one year, or reserving yearly rent. Under Section 49 of the Registration Act, an unregistered document required to be registered cannot affect the property or be received as evidence of the transaction, subject to the stated proviso. The Court relied on Smt. Shantabai v. State of Bombay, Satish Chand Makhan v. Govardhan Das Byas, and Bajaj Auto Limited v. Behari Lal Kohli.

predicates.compulsory_registration_lease_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an instrument purporting to grant a lease created that lease.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The parties did not register the instrument purporting to grant the lease.
predicates.lease_document_requires_registration: The purported lease is of a kind for which the law requires a registered instrument.

issues.definition: When a lease-instrument dispute concerns an unregistered instrument that requires registration, the instrument cannot create or prove the purported lease.

issues.legal_issue: A tenancy may arise from the parties’ conduct even when an unregistered instrument cannot create the lease it purports to record.
material_facts: The owner inducted the occupant into possession of the building.
The occupant paid monthly rent, and the parties’ conduct showed that rent was payable for the building.
The owner transferred legal possession to the occupant, and the record did not support treating the possession as merely permissive.
Although the parties had executed an unregistered instrument purporting to grant a five-year lease, the surrounding facts showed an intention to create a lease.
issues.conclusion: The parties’ conduct established a lease independent of the unregistered instrument; because the instrument could not create a lease exceeding one year, the tenancy arising from the conduct was one falling within the residual mode in Section 107, second paragraph, of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act defines a lease as a transfer of a right to enjoy property for consideration, and permits the transfer to be made expressly or by implication. Section 107, second paragraph, permits other leases to be made by oral agreement accompanied by delivery of possession. The Court relied on Technicians Studio Pvt. Ltd. v. Lila Ghosh for the principle that intention to create a tenancy is determined from the facts and circumstances, and distinguished H.S. Rikhy v. New Delhi Municipal Corporation. It also noted that its conclusion was consistent with Biswabani Pvt. Ltd. v. Santosh Kumar Dutta.

rule.if: lease_status_dispute and owner_inducted_occupant_into_possession and legal_possession_transferred and rent_paid_or_agreed and conduct_indicates_intended_lease and not possession_shown_to_be_merely_permissive

predicates.lease_status_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an occupant holds the property as a lessee.
predicates.owner_inducted_occupant_into_possession: The owner placed the occupant in possession of the property.
predicates.legal_possession_transferred: The owner transferred legal possession of the property to the occupant.
predicates.rent_paid_or_agreed: The occupant paid rent or agreed to pay rent for use of the property.
predicates.conduct_indicates_intended_lease: The parties’ conduct indicates that they intended to transfer a right to enjoy the property in return for rent.
predicates.possession_shown_to_be_merely_permissive: The evidence shows that the occupant’s possession was merely permissive, without a tenancy relationship.

issues.definition: When an owner has inducted an occupant into legal possession, rent is paid or agreed, the parties’ conduct indicates an intended lease, and the possession is not shown to be merely permissive, a tenancy arises independently of an ineffective instrument.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant protected by rent-control legislation cannot be evicted through an ordinary civil suit where the legislation requires eviction to be pursued before the rent-control forum.
material_facts: The occupant held the building under a tenancy arising from the owner’s transfer of possession and the payment or agreement to pay rent.
The Rent Act defined a tenant by reference to rent payable for a building and applied to buildings let or to be let.
The landlord brought an ordinary civil suit to recover possession rather than seeking eviction before the Rent Control Court.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was a tenant protected by the Rent Act, the civil court could not grant the requested eviction, and the suit was dismissed without prejudice to the landlord’s right to seek relief under the Rent Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(6) and 2(i) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, define tenant and building in terms that require a lease and rent payable for the building. Once a tenancy is established, the Act governs eviction and the landlord must seek eviction before the Rent Control Court on a ground recognised by the Act. The Court relied on Biswabani Pvt. Ltd. v. Santosh Kumar Dutta in recognising continued statutory protection under rent-control legislation.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brings an ordinary civil suit seeking to recover possession from an occupant.
predicates.tenancy_established: The occupant holds the property under a landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.rent_control_law_covers_the_tenancy: The applicable rent-control law covers the building and the established tenancy.

issues.definition: If an ordinary civil suit seeks eviction from a tenancy covered by rent-control law, eviction must be sought before the rent-control forum.
